thread.title: Kroger Could Deliver for Investors, Says Bill Priest

author: barrons.com
title: Kroger Could Deliver for Investors, Says Bill Priest
text:
William Priest Photo: Jeremy Liebman July 13, 2018 8:06 p.m. ET Barron’s : What do you make of this market, Bill?
William Priest: The outlook for earnings and dividends is excellent this year. There will be a substantial increase in earnings, due in part to the corporate tax cuts enacted late last year. With regard to dividends—whether paid in cash or through stock buybacks—this will be one of the best years ever. But those two positives conflict with a negative: the likelihood that stocks’ price/earnings ratios will contract as the Federal Reserve moves from QE to QT. [Quantitative easing, or asset-buying, increased the money supply to stimulate the economy; quantitative tightening is the reverse.] The Fed artificially lowered the discount rate for all financial assets, but now you’ll see the discount rate increase. The stock market could be much more volatile under QT than QE.
Two big issues face the market. The budget deficit will come in at just over $1 trillion next year. That’s about 5% of GDP, a record excluding wars and recessions. But then add Fed QE redemptions of about $200 billion, and that brings Treasury financings up to 6% of GDP. This is worrisome, even without including the wall of investment-grade and high-yield corporate bond maturities (roughly $0.7 trillion and $0.3 trillion, respectively).
Second, the trade backdrop is troubling. No one wins a trade war. There are some legitimate issues with regard to China’s trade policies, but I had hoped they would have been handled on a more constructive bilateral basis. A full-blown trade war isn’t good for investing.
To sum up, we expect a highly volatile market, with a slight upward bias. The geopolitical backdrop is more negative than positive, but how low can stocks go with S&P 500 earnings of $175 for the year?
William Priest’s Report Card
Are you finding compelling investments in this market?
Well, I wish I hadn’t recommended some of my January picks. We sold our Starbucks [ticker: SBUX] position in the first quarter because the same-store sales recovery isn’t materializing as quickly or strongly as we had envisioned. We also closed out our MetLife [MET] position in the second quarter, as a lack of internal momentum, coupled with a flattening yield curve, could become an issue. Applied Materials [AMAT] is down about 10% this year, hurt by the trade talk, but we continue to like it. The company has guided for better sales and gross profit margins, and bought back $2.5 billion of stock in the latest quarter. Applied is gaining market share. We are also hanging on to Martin Marietta Materials [MLM]. We recommended it at $227; it later fell to around $200 and we bought a little more. Now it’s back to the $227 area.

The stock has fallen 50%, to $87, since our January get-together.
We still like it a lot. The company supplies technology for organic light-emitting diodes used in mobile phones, computers, TVs, and other devices. Universal Display has suffered because Apple ’s [AAPL] iPhone X sales have been a bit disappointing. Also, near-term, the company hasn’t yet been able to develop a blue emitter [for producing very high-quality images on displays]. But long-term, the story is intact. Recently, it was reported that Samsung Electronics [005930.Korea] and Canon Tokki are working on blue OLED TV equipment. That’s a positive development. Our near-term price target for Universal Display is $120.
How about some new ideas?
We bought Kroger [KR], the supermarket operator, for around $24 a share. The stock is about $28 now. Kroger should generate roughly $15 billion of operating cash flow over the next three years. Capital spending could total $9 billion. The company will return $6 billion to shareholders, or roughly 25% of the current market capitalization, using a meaningful portion of its free cash flow to repurchase shares. That could increase the disparity between analysts’ earnings estimates and Kroger’s own earnings guidance beyond fiscal 2019. We think Kroger can earn between $2 a share and $2.15 in the current fiscal year [ending next January], and see that growing to $2.60 or maybe even $3 in fiscal 2020.
How does Kroger plan to stay competitive with Amazon.com [AMZN], which owns Whole Foods Market?
Kroger has de-risked itself with regard to potential disintermediation from e-commerce and created an underappreciated future incremental growth opportunity. It recently made a significant investment in Ocado Group [OCDO.UK], a British online grocer, and will license Ocado’s warehouse automation and grocery-distribution technology. We think Kroger’s shares could double.
Phillips 66 [PSX], my next idea, is emerging as a global swing supplier of both refined petroleum products and polyethylene. Its strategic access to discounted landlocked crude oil, and its advantageous supplies of natural-gas liquids have positioned Phillips as the low-cost producer, and should lead to a paradigm shift in its ability to arbitrage demand among the U.S., the southern hemisphere, and Asia. Pricing differentials between West Texas intermediate crude and landlocked crude oil in Canada and the Permian Basin will allow Phillips to fully recover its fixed cost on roughly 500,000 to 600,000 barrels, allowing it to earn a high variable profit rate on the balance of its 1.6 million barrels of daily refining capacity.
Does the price of oil matter to your case?
This is a margin-expansion story. The sale of LPG [liquefied petroleum gas] byproducts from its NGL [natural gas liquid] fractionation will allow Phillips’ chemical joint venture, which is overlooked by many analysts, to recover a substantial portion of its feedstock costs. We think the company could capture almost all the profit margin embedded in its polyethylene production. Phillips could earn well over $7 a share in 2018, and perhaps as much as $12 in 2019. The stock is trading for $111. It could go to $160.
Thank you, Bill.
